questions.question: What is the difference between controlled and uncontrolled form fields in React?
questions.title: Controlled vs Uncontrolled Form Fields
questions.direct_answer: A controlled field gets its current value from React state through `value` or `checked` and updates that state in `onChange`. An uncontrolled field keeps its current value in the DOM; React may provide only an initial `defaultValue` or `defaultChecked`, and the application reads the value when needed with `FormData` or a ref.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether value ownership, prop choice, and update flow are understood.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling uncontrolled fields unvalidated or treating controlled as universally better.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Choose per field and explain the DOM-versus-state ownership boundary.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Controlled: React state is the source of truth for the current value.
Uncontrolled: the DOM keeps the current value after the initial render.
Use `value` or `checked` with a synchronous `onChange` for controlled fields.
Use `defaultValue` or `defaultChecked` for an uncontrolled initial value.
A single form can use both styles when different fields have different needs.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A controlled form field receives its current value from React. A text input uses `value`, while a checkbox or radio uses `checked`. Its `onChange` handler immediately writes the user’s edit back to state, so the rendered value and the state value stay together.

An uncontrolled field lets the browser DOM keep the current value. React can set its starting value with `defaultValue` or `defaultChecked`, but later typing does not update React state. On submit, the application can read named fields with `FormData`, or it can use a ref for a specific DOM operation.

For example, a live product search is naturally controlled because the result list changes after every keystroke. A simple notes field that is needed only when the form is submitted can remain uncontrolled and be read from the submitted form.

Neither style is automatically more correct. Controlled fields make live validation, conditional UI, formatting, and resets straightforward, but each state update can re-render their owner. Uncontrolled fields reduce state wiring, but other components cannot reliably react to every edit without reading the DOM.

The useful distinction is ownership: React owns a controlled value; the DOM owns an uncontrolled value. Choose per field according to when the application needs the current value, and remember that a file input’s selected files are read from the DOM rather than assigned as a normal controlled value.

sections.title: The current value has one owner
sections.content: A field may begin with the same text in both styles, but the update path differs. With a controlled field, an edit becomes an event, then state, then a rendered prop. With an uncontrolled field, the browser changes the DOM value directly and React usually reads it only at a boundary such as form submission.

sections.title: Controlled form input lifecycle
sections.content:
In the controlled path, the browser reports an edit through `onChange`. The handler stores `event.target.value` or `event.target.checked`, React renders again, and the input receives that stored value. Because state changes on every edit, nearby UI can derive a character count, disable a button, filter a list, or validate another field without querying the DOM.

In the uncontrolled path, `defaultValue` is only the starting point. After mounting, the browser owns what the user types. A submit handler can construct `new FormData(event.currentTarget)` and read every successful named control. A ref is more suitable when the code needs the element itself, such as focusing it; it should not become a second shadow state store.

The styles can be mixed deliberately. The important rule is that one field should not alternate owners during the same mounted lifetime. Also use the correct prop family: `checked` for checkboxes and radios, not their `value` prop, which describes the submitted value rather than whether they are selected.

sections.title: Who stores and updates the current value?
sections.content:
| Question | Controlled field | Uncontrolled field |
|---|---|---|
| Current value lives in | React state | Browser DOM |
| Initial/current prop | `value` or `checked` | `defaultValue` or `defaultChecked` |
| Read on every edit | `onChange` updates state | Usually unnecessary |
| Read on submit | State or `FormData` | `FormData` or ref |
| Best fit | Live UI depends on the value | Collect the value at a boundary |

sections.title: Use each ownership model for a field that fits it

questions.question: When should you use controlled or uncontrolled fields in a React form?
questions.title: Choosing the Right Form Field Model
questions.direct_answer: Use a controlled field when the interface must know or change its value while the user types, such as live search, dependent fields, formatting, or immediate validation. Use an uncontrolled field when the browser can hold the value until submit, or when working with file inputs and DOM-focused integrations. The choice can be made field by field.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the model is selected from interaction requirements rather than habit.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using React state for submit-only data or avoiding it when live UI needs the value.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Separate ownership choice from validation and component-level performance design.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Choose controlled when other UI depends on the value now.
Choose uncontrolled when the value is only collected at submit.
Controlled fields simplify programmatic changes, resets, and cross-field rules.
Uncontrolled fields need less React state and work naturally with `FormData`.
Keep rapidly updating state close to the field if re-rendering becomes expensive.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The decision depends on when the application needs the field’s current value. I use a controlled field when an edit must immediately affect rendered UI, another field, or a business rule. React state then provides one current value that every dependent part of the component can read.

For example, a delivery selector can be controlled because choosing express delivery changes the price summary and may reveal an address field. A coupon input is also often controlled when the UI shows its status or clears it after the coupon is applied.

I use an uncontrolled field when the browser can collect the value until a natural boundary. A basic contact form can give its fields names and read them with `FormData` on submit. That avoids creating state and change handlers that no rendered UI needs. File inputs are also read through their files collection.

Controlled does not mean that an entire page must re-render on each keypress. The state can live in a small form component, expensive dependent work can be deferred, and a form library can subscribe more narrowly. Uncontrolled also does not mean unvalidated; native constraints or submit-time validation still apply.

I therefore choose the smallest ownership model that supports the interaction. Live coordination points toward controlled fields; collect-at-submit data points toward uncontrolled fields. Mixing them is fine as long as each mounted field keeps one model consistently.

sections.title: Decide from the interaction, not from a blanket rule
sections.content: Ask whether another part of the interface needs the value before submission. If yes, state gives React a dependable value to render from. If no, the browser’s form model may already provide everything needed. Performance is a component-design concern, not a reason to declare one model universally better.

sections.title: Four signals make the choice clearer
sections.content:
Immediate derivation is the strongest controlled signal. Character counters, live previews, conditional sections, and synchronized inputs all require the render to observe each edit. Programmatic control is another signal: if an external action must set, normalize, or clear the value, state gives that action an explicit place to write.

Submit-only collection is the strongest uncontrolled signal. The browser already tracks text, selections, and checked states and can serialize successful named controls. That is often enough for small forms. DOM-owned widgets and file selectors are also natural boundaries because their useful value is exposed through the element or an integration API.

Validation alone does not settle the choice. Both styles can use HTML constraints, and both can run custom validation. The real question is whether validation feedback must be derived continuously or only after blur or submit. When controlled keystrokes make a large tree slow, isolate the form state instead of changing ownership without understanding the interaction.

sections.title: A field-by-field decision path
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Does rendered UI need the current value before submit?] -->|Yes| B[Use a controlled field]
  A -->|No| C[Must code set or reset it programmatically?]
  C -->|Yes| B
  C -->|No| D[Is it a file or DOM-owned integration?]
  D -->|Yes| E[Use an uncontrolled field or adapter]
  D -->|No| F[Collect it with FormData at submit]
  B --> G[Keep value defined and update synchronously]
```

questions.question: Why does React warn when an input switches between controlled and uncontrolled?
questions.title: Controlled and Uncontrolled Switch Warnings
questions.direct_answer: React warns because one mounted input must keep the same value owner for its lifetime. Passing `undefined` first leaves a text input uncontrolled; later passing a string makes it controlled. Initialize controlled text with an empty string and controlled checkboxes with a boolean, or keep the field uncontrolled and use a default prop throughout.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the first-render ownership contract and missing-value bug are understood.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Fixing the warning with remounting instead of keeping a stable defined value.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain string and boolean normalization plus synchronous controlled updates.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: A mounted field cannot switch between controlled and uncontrolled modes.
Initialize controlled text state with `""` and checkbox state with `false`.
Use `value={possiblyMissing ?? ""}` when data may be absent.
A controlled editable field also needs a synchronous `onChange` handler.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The warning means the owner of a mounted input changed. A text input without a defined `value` is uncontrolled, so the browser owns its current text. If a later render supplies a string `value`, React is suddenly asked to own the same field. That ambiguous transition can overwrite user edits or create inconsistent behavior.

A common cause is data that arrives after the first render. For example, `useState()` produces `undefined` initially, then an API result sets the name to `"Asha"`. The input starts uncontrolled and becomes controlled when the result arrives.

The fix is to decide the model at initialization. A controlled text input should always receive a string, often with `useState("")` or `value={name ?? ""}`. A controlled checkbox should always receive a boolean. An intentionally uncontrolled field should use `defaultValue` or `defaultChecked` and should not receive a later current-value prop.

There is a related warning when `value` or `checked` is provided without an `onChange` handler: React renders a read-only field unless `readOnly` is intentional. An editable controlled field must update its backing state synchronously from the change event.

The durable rule is one owner for one mounted lifetime. Normalize missing data before it reaches a controlled prop, and use default props only for fields whose current value remains in the DOM.

sections.title: The first render establishes the ownership contract
sections.content: React decides whether a field is controlled from the current-value prop it receives. A defined text `value` or boolean `checked` creates a controlled field. If that prop is absent or undefined, the field is uncontrolled. Later renders must preserve that choice until the element unmounts.

sections.title: Missing values are data states, but not valid controlled text values
sections.content:
Applications often represent loading data with `undefined` or `null`. That state is useful in application logic, but a controlled text input needs a string on every render. Convert the missing state at the boundary with `profile?.name ?? ""`, or keep separate loading UI until a stable initial value exists. For checkboxes, normalize to a boolean rather than falling back to a string.

A different mistake is passing `value` together with an unrelated or delayed update. React re-applies the supplied value, so typing appears frozen or the caret jumps. The immediate change handler should store the DOM’s new value; expensive search or formatting work can happen separately without delaying ownership of the input.

Changing a component `key` can hide the warning by remounting the element, but it also discards selection, focus, and local DOM state. Remount only when a new logical field is intended. For normal data loading, keep the component mounted and keep its controlled value type stable.

sections.title: How the warning appears and how the stable path differs
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[first render: value is undefined] --> B[DOM owns the input]
  B --> C[later render: value is a string]
  C --> D[ownership switch warning]
  E[first render: value is empty string] --> F[React owns the input]
  F --> G[onChange stores each edit]
  G --> H[later render: value stays a string]
```

sections.title: Keep controlled values defined from the first render
